blocks.text: No one has explained the meaning of the word פרודות better, and at the same time weighed its various interpretations more carefully, than Edward Pococke in his Commentary. Since I see that it is almost neglected today and in the hands of few, though undeservedly, for it is full of solid and exquisite learning, I shall add from it what is most to the point. "From the root פרד, which among the Hebrews, Chaldeans and Arabs means to separate or to be separated, nouns can be derived that denote something single and separated from others, such as grains of corn and the seed that is sown and committed to the earth. And it is not absurd that the Hebrew noun can be taken in this sense here too, [III, 301] although its form is quite peculiar, since it is nowhere used in Holy Scripture as a substantive, nor does any other occurrence of it appear, as with the Syriac ܦܪܕܐ, which occurs in the version of the N. T. in the sense of grain or seed sown, and in the plural grains or seeds sown. Hence it appears that it was not without weighty reason rendered thus, and explained by some of the Jews as גרגרי החטה והשערה, grains of wheat and barley, or גרגרי הזרע, grains of seed, which are sown, separated and scattered over the ground; or, as Abu Walid puts it in Arabic, الحبوب المبذورات للزراعة [al-ḥubūb al-mabdhūrāt li-l-zirāʿa], grains scattered in sowing; and R. Tanchum, الحبوب المعدودة للزراعة لانها تغرق في الارض [al-ḥubūb al-maʿdūda li-l-zirāʿa li-annahā tughraq fī al-arḍ], grains prepared for sowing, so called because they are scattered over the ground. The author of the Arabic manuscript [he means the Arabic version of the O. T., which he possessed and often cites, and which he thinks was composed by R. Saadia Haggaon, in the Preface, p. 16] assigns it the same meaning and derives it from the same root, rendering it المتفردات [al-mutafarridāt] (which literally means separated), where in a special note he explains that he understands קמח אלבדאר אלדי הו קמח מפרד לם פיה זואן, seed wheat, which is separated wheat, with which no darnel is mixed, לאן כאן דאב אלנאס יבדדו אלגל מן אלקמח, because it is the custom of men to sow the choicest (or most select) of the wheat. Abarbinel too takes it so, but he also adduces the reason for the meaning, namely, not that one grain is separated and distinct from another, or set apart from darnel, but that the seed is separated (or withdrawn) from the eyes of men and hidden in the recesses of the soil. And thus all these agree in the same meaning and the same root of the noun, however much they waver somewhat in the explanation of the derivation." So Pococke.
